literal: the mind looks about to go haywire

entry.literal: the mind looks about to go haywire
entry.use: Exaggerated frustration at noise, heat, waiting or a person: kono oto, ki ga kuruisou. Ki ga kurutta no? (have you lost your mind?) is the other form you'll hear. It's strong and TV tends to avoid it, so atama ga okashiku narisou is the softer everyday swap.

example.romaji: tonari no kouji, urusakute ki ga kuruisou.
example.ja: 隣の工事、うるさくて気が狂いそう。
example.english: The construction next door is so loud it's driving me crazy.

examplePolite.romaji: kou atsui to ki ga kuruisou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: こう暑いと気が狂いそうですね。
examplePolite.english: This heat is enough to drive you mad.

entry.notes: Softer: atama ga okashiku narisou; ki ga kurutta no? = have you lost your mind?

entry.use: Ends an argument when you give up on persuading someone: mou ii, katte ni shite. The rough male katte ni shiro is the form films use most, and katte ni sureba (go ahead, then) is colder. Suki ni shite is the friendly 'do as you like'.

example.romaji: mou ii, katte ni shite.
example.ja: もういい、勝手にして。
example.english: Forget it. Do whatever you want.

examplePolite.romaji: wakarimashita. jaa, katte ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: わかりました。じゃあ、勝手にしてください。
examplePolite.english: Fine. Suit yourself, then.

entry.notes: Rough: katte ni shiro; colder: katte ni sureba.

entry.kana: こころのじゅんびができる
entry.use: Mostly negative, when news or a big moment comes too fast: mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai. Kokoro no junbi wa ii? asks if someone is ready to hear something. Plain junbi ga dekiru is being ready in practical terms.

example.romaji: chotto matte, mada kokoro no junbi ga dekitenai.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、まだ心の準備ができてない。
example.english: Wait, I'm not ready for this yet.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni iwarete mo, kokoro no junbi ga dekite imasen.
examplePolite.ja: 急に言われても、心の準備ができていません。
examplePolite.english: You can't spring that on me. I'm not ready.

entry.notes: Also: kokoro no junbi o suru (brace yourself).

entry.use: The stock gloat at someone getting their comeuppance, often said jokingly among friends or muttered at a rival; zamaa! on its own is common too. Ii kimi is the quieter 'serves them right', said about someone rather than at them.

example.romaji: warikonda kuruma, tsukamatteru. zamaa miro.
example.ja: 割り込んだ車、捕まってる。ざまあみろ。
example.english: The car that cut in got pulled over. Serves him right.

entry.notes: Also: zamaa!, zama miro.

entry.use: Quiet satisfaction when someone who had it coming slips up, usually ii kimi da: said about someone more than to them, unlike zamaa miro. The kimi here is 'feeling' (as in kimi ga warui), not kimi 'you'.

example.romaji: itsumo ibatteta kara, ii kimi da yo.
example.ja: いつも威張ってたから、いい気味だよ。
example.english: He was always so full of himself, so serves him right.

entry.use: Doing something rash after a breakup, a failure or bad news because nothing seems to matter, mostly as the warning yake ni naranaide (don't do anything stupid). Tohou ni kureru is being stuck and helpless; yake ni naru is lashing out.

example.romaji: ikkai shippai shita kurai de, yake ni naranaide yo.
example.ja: 一回失敗したくらいで、ヤケにならないでよ。
example.english: Don't go off the rails just because you failed once.

examplePolite.romaji: yake ni naranaide, mou ichido kangaete mimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ヤケにならないで、もう一度考えてみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Don't do anything rash. Let's think it over again.

entry.notes: yakekuso (desperate, all-or-nothing); yakezake (drinking to drown it).

literal: the mind clears up (like the sky)

entry.literal: the mind clears up (like the sky)
entry.use: Said after venting, a good cry or a change of scene, usually in the past: hanashitara ki ga hareta. Ki ga magireru only takes your mind off a worry for a while; ki ga hareru means it actually lifts.

example.romaji: omoikkiri naitara, chotto ki ga hareta.
example.ja: 思いっきり泣いたら、ちょっと気が晴れた。
example.english: I had a good cry and feel a bit better.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi o kiite moratte, sukoshi ki ga haremashita.
examplePolite.ja: 話を聞いてもらって、少し気が晴れました。
examplePolite.english: Having you listen made me feel a little better.

entry.notes: Single word for a pick-me-up: kibarashi.

entry.use: A complaint about a tense or controlling home, office or relationship: ano ie, iki ga tsumaru, often as iki ga tsumarisou. It can also be literal, not being able to breathe.

example.romaji: jikka ni zutto iru to, iki ga tsumaru.
example.ja: 実家にずっといると、息が詰まる。
example.english: Being at my parents' the whole time is suffocating.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kaigi, iki ga tsumarisou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: あの会議、息が詰まりそうでした。
examplePolite.english: That meeting was suffocating.

entry.notes: Single word: ikigurushii (stifling).

literal: night falls on the way ahead

entry.literal: night falls on the way ahead
entry.use: Being stranded with no idea what to do next, mostly in the past: saifu nakushite tohou ni kureta. It's helpless rather than upset; yake ni naru is lashing out in despair.

example.romaji: shuuden nogashite, tohou ni kureta.
example.ja: 終電逃して、途方に暮れた。
example.english: I missed the last train and had no idea what to do.

examplePolite.romaji: saifu o nakushite, tohou ni kurete imashita.
examplePolite.ja: 財布をなくして、途方に暮れていました。
examplePolite.english: I'd lost my wallet and was completely at a loss.

entry.notes: Not kureru 'give'; casual alternative: dou shiyou.

english: get fed up, be sick of it
literal: a feeling of dislike creeps in

entry.english: get fed up, be sick of it
entry.literal: a feeling of dislike creeps in
entry.englishIdiom: be sick and tired of it
entry.use: Said about a job, a place, a routine or yourself, often as iyake ga sashite kita (I'm getting sick of it): shigoto ni iyake ga sasu. Akiru is being bored of something; iyake ga sasu is real dislike.

example.romaji: mainichi onaji koto no kurikaeshi de, iyake ga sashite kita.
example.ja: 毎日同じことの繰り返しで、嫌気がさしてきた。
example.english: Same thing every day. I'm getting sick of it.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, ima no shigoto ni iyake ga sashite imasu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、今の仕事に嫌気がさしています。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm fed up with my job.

entry.notes: Plain word: unzari suru (be fed up).

english: beat yourself up over it, brood
literal: fall ill in the mind over it

entry.english: beat yourself up over it, brood
entry.literal: fall ill in the mind over it
entry.use: Almost always the comfort line ki ni yamanaide (don't let it eat at you), to someone blaming themselves. Ki ni suru is everyday minding; ki ni yamu is brooding until it hurts.

example.romaji: anata no sei ja nai n da kara, ki ni yamanaide.
example.ja: あなたのせいじゃないんだから、気に病まないで。
example.english: It's not your fault, so don't beat yourself up over it.

examplePolite.romaji: amari ki ni yamanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: あまり気に病まないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please don't let it weigh on you too much.

entry.notes: Everyday version: ki ni shinaide.

entry.use: The awkward feeling of being caught out or having to face someone after a slip, often in the past: uso ga barete kimari ga warukatta. Batsu ga warui means the same and is just as common; hazukashii is plain embarrassment.

example.romaji: uso ga barete, sugoku kimari ga warukatta.
example.ja: 嘘がバレて、すごくきまりが悪かった。
example.english: My lie got found out and I felt so sheepish.

examplePolite.romaji: onaji hito ni nido mo ayamaru no wa, kimari ga warui desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 同じ人に二度も謝るのは、きまりが悪いですね。
examplePolite.english: Apologising to the same person twice is a bit awkward.

entry.notes: Same meaning: batsu ga warui.

english: it pains me, it breaks my heart

entry.english: it pains me, it breaks my heart
entry.use: Said about sad news, someone's hardship, or guilt at hurting someone: aa iu nyuusu o miru to mune ga itamu. Kokoro ga itamu means the same and is heard as often. Mune ga itai can also be literal chest pain.

example.romaji: aa iu nyuusu o miru to, mune ga itamu yo ne.
example.ja: ああいうニュースを見ると、胸が痛むよね。
example.english: News like that really breaks your heart.

examplePolite.romaji: hisaichi no eizou o miru to, mune ga itamimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 被災地の映像を見ると、胸が痛みます。
examplePolite.english: Seeing footage of the disaster area pains me.

entry.notes: Same meaning: kokoro ga itamu.

literal: strike out at all eight sides

entry.literal: strike out at all eight sides
entry.use: Venting your bad mood on someone who had nothing to do with it, mostly in the complaint yatsuatari shinaide yo or the apology gomen, yatsuatari shita. The noun works alone too: sore, tada no yatsuatari ja n.

example.romaji: kocchi ni yatsuatari shinaide yo.
example.ja: こっちに八つ当たりしないでよ。
example.english: Don't take it out on me.

examplePolite.romaji: sakki wa yatsuatari shite, sumimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: さっきは八つ当たりして、すみませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Sorry for taking it out on you earlier.

entry.politeJa: 気持ちを切り替えます
entry.use: Said after a loss, a mistake or a bad day to move on to the next thing, often as kimochi kirikaete ikou. Shinki itten is a whole fresh start; kimochi o kirikaeru is a quick reset.

example.romaji: maketa no wa shouganai. kimochi kirikaete tsugi ikou.
example.ja: 負けたのはしょうがない。気持ち切り替えて次行こう。
example.english: Losing can't be helped. Shake it off and on to the next one.

examplePolite.romaji: kimochi o kirikaete, mata ganbarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 気持ちを切り替えて、また頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll put it behind me and keep at it.

entry.notes: Noun: kirikae (kirikae ga hayai = bounces back fast).

entry.polite: ki ga ki ja nai desu
entry.use: Anxious waiting, when you can't settle until you hear news, often in the past: kekka ga deru made ki ga ki ja nakatta. Munasawagi ga suru is a hunch something's wrong; ki ga ki ja nai is fretting over something you already know about.

example.romaji: kekka ga deru made, ki ga ki ja nakatta.
example.ja: 結果が出るまで、気が気じゃなかった。
example.english: I was a nervous wreck until the results came out.

examplePolite.romaji: renraku ga kuru made, ki ga ki ja nakatta desu.
examplePolite.ja: 連絡が来るまで、気が気じゃなかったです。
examplePolite.english: I was on pins and needles until I heard from you.

entry.notes: Slightly formal: ki ga ki de nai; plain word: shinpai.

entry.use: A rough reaction to a nasty story, an unfair ending or a bully: munakuso warui hanashi da na. The disgust is moral, not physical; kimochi warui is the physical 'gross'.

example.romaji: ano nyuusu, hontou ni munakuso warui.
example.ja: あのニュース、本当に胸くそ悪い。
example.english: That news is genuinely sickening.

entry.notes: Slang short form: munakuso.

entry.englishIdiom: have a bad feeling about this
entry.use: A sense that something is wrong before you know it, built like ki ga suru: nanka munasawagi ga suru. Often when someone can't be reached or something feels off.

example.romaji: nanka iya na munasawagi ga suru.
example.ja: なんか嫌な胸騒ぎがする。
example.english: I've got a bad feeling about this.

examplePolite.romaji: renraku ga tsukanakute, munasawagi ga shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 連絡がつかなくて、胸騒ぎがします。
examplePolite.english: I can't reach them, and I have a bad feeling.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: iya na yokan ga suru.

literal: the heart's workings turn over once

entry.literal: the heart's workings turn over once
entry.use: Said at a new job, a move, a new school year or New Year, usually leading the sentence: shinki itten, ganbarimasu. Kimochi o kirikaeru is a quick reset after a setback; shinki itten is a whole fresh start.

example.romaji: shinki itten, atarashii heya de ganbaru.
example.ja: 心機一転、新しい部屋で頑張る。
example.english: Fresh start: new place, new effort.

examplePolite.romaji: shinki itten, ganbarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 心機一転、頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'm making a fresh start.

entry.use: A comic reaction to something absurd or unexpected, almost always in the past: sono kotae ni me ga ten ni natta. It comes from manga, where shocked eyes shrink to dots. Atama ga masshiro ni naru is freezing up; me ga ten is staring in disbelief.

example.romaji: kare no kotae ni, me ga ten ni natta.
example.ja: 彼の答えに、目が点になった。
example.english: His answer left me speechless.

examplePolite.romaji: nedan o kiite, me ga ten ni narimashita.
examplePolite.ja: 値段を聞いて、目が点になりました。
examplePolite.english: When I heard the price, I was dumbfounded.

english: a smooth talker, good at flattery

entry.english: a smooth talker, good at flattery
entry.use: A warning about a salesperson or charmer who talks people round (kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete), or a laughing reply to a compliment: mata, kuchi ga umai n da kara. Not umai alone (tasty, good at).

example.romaji: kare, kuchi ga umai kara ki o tsukete.
example.ja: 彼、口がうまいから気をつけて。
example.english: He's a smooth talker, so watch out.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa kuchi ga umai node, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は口がうまいので、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: He's a smooth talker, so do be careful.

entry.notes: Also kuchi ga jouzu; written 口が上手い too.

entry.use: The host's line when serving food, politely with o: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen kedo; and the guest's soft way to decline: chotto kuchi ni awanakute. Shou ni au is for activities, not food.

example.romaji: kore, kuchi ni au ka wakannai kedo, tabete mite.
example.ja: これ、口に合うかわかんないけど、食べてみて。
example.english: Not sure you'll like it, but give it a try.

examplePolite.romaji: okuchi ni au ka wakarimasen ga, douzo.
examplePolite.ja: お口に合うかわかりませんが、どうぞ。
examplePolite.english: I'm not sure it'll be to your taste, but please have some.

entry.notes: Polite with o: okuchi ni au; plain way: suki ka wakannai (not sure you'll like it).

english: a loner who goes their own way

entry.english: a loner who goes their own way
entry.use: About a coworker or classmate who works alone and keeps out of groups, said neutrally or with a little admiration: kare wa ippiki ookami da kara. Often softened with tte kanji (kind of a lone wolf).

example.romaji: kare tte, ippiki ookami tte kanji da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼って、一匹狼って感じだよね。
example.english: He's kind of a lone wolf, isn't he?

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa ippiki ookami tte kanji desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼は一匹狼って感じですよね。
examplePolite.english: He's a bit of a lone wolf, isn't he?

entry.notes: Plain way: hitori de iru no ga suki (likes being on their own).

entry.use: A complaint about a parent, partner or boss who won't hear any advice or objection, usually with o dropped: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai. Always negative; it's refusing to listen, not being unable to hear (kikoenai).

example.romaji: nani itte mo kiku mimi motanai n da yo.
example.ja: 何言っても聞く耳持たないんだよ。
example.english: Whatever I say, he just won't listen.

examplePolite.romaji: nani o itte mo kiku mimi o motanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 何を言っても聞く耳を持たないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: No matter what I say, he won't listen.

entry.notes: Plain way: zenzen kiite kurenai (just won't listen to me).

entry.use: Grudging admiration for someone who covers every angle or grabs every advantage, like a coworker who has already booked the good meeting room: nukeme nai na, with ga dropped. Sharper than youryou ga ii, and it can hint at calculating.

example.romaji: ano hito, honto nukeme nai yo ne.
example.ja: あの人、ほんと抜け目ないよね。
example.english: She never misses a trick.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito wa hontou ni nukeme ga nai desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人は本当に抜け目がないですよね。
examplePolite.english: She really never misses a chance, does she?

entry.notes: Adverb: nukeme naku (shrewdly, without missing a thing).

entry.use: Praise, often grudging, for a sharp strategist, lawyer, boss or rival; before a noun, atama no kireru hito. Not kireru alone, which means snap or lose it (ano hito sugu kireru).

example.romaji: ano bengoshi, atama kireru yo.
example.ja: あの弁護士、頭切れるよ。
example.english: That lawyer's really sharp.

examplePolite.romaji: ano bengoshi-san wa atama ga kiremasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの弁護士さんは頭が切れますよ。
examplePolite.english: That lawyer is very sharp.

entry.notes: Plain: atama ga ii (smart); kireru alone = snap, lose your temper.

entry.use: Praise for someone who forgives mistakes or lets things go, like a partner who laughs off a forgotten anniversary: kokoro hiroi ne. The opposite kokoro ga semai (petty) is a common jab.

example.romaji: sore de yurushita no? kokoro hiroi ne.
example.ja: それで許したの？心広いね。
example.english: You forgave him for that? You're so big-hearted.

examplePolite.romaji: sore de yurushita n desu ka? kokoro ga hiroi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それで許したんですか？心が広いですね。
examplePolite.english: You forgave him for that? That's big of you.

entry.notes: Opposite: kokoro ga semai (petty, narrow-minded).

entry.use: About someone who changes completely when drunk, angry or behind the wheel (nomu to hito ga kawaru), or someone who has changed for good or bad: hito ga kawatta mitai. Mostly with -to or in the past.

example.romaji: kare, osake nomu to hito ga kawaru n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お酒飲むと人が変わるんだよ。
example.english: He turns into a different person when he drinks.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa osake o nomu to hito ga kawaru n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお酒を飲むと人が変わるんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He becomes a different person when he drinks.

entry.notes: Like a different person: hito ga kawatta you ni / mitai ni.

entry.use: The staple complaint about a boss, clerk or system that won't make an exception: yuuzuu kikanai na. Mostly negative; yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible) is praise. Atama ga katai is about ideas; this is about rules and requests.

example.romaji: uchi no buchou, honto yuuzuu kikanai n da yo.
example.ja: うちの部長、ほんと融通利かないんだよ。
example.english: My boss just won't bend the rules.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no buchou wa hontou ni yuuzuu ga kikanai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: うちの部長は本当に融通が利かないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Our manager really won't make any exceptions.

entry.notes: Opposite: yuuzuu ga kiku (flexible, accommodating).

english: jumping the gun, getting ahead of oneself

entry.english: jumping the gun, getting ahead of oneself
entry.use: A light tease for someone planning or celebrating too early, like booking the honeymoon before the proposal: mada ki ga hayai yo. Not ki ga mijikai (short-tempered).

example.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi? ki ga hayai ne.
example.ja: もうクリスマスの準備？気が早いね。
example.english: Getting ready for Christmas already? Bit early, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: mou kurisumasu no junbi desu ka? ki ga hayai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: もうクリスマスの準備ですか？気が早いですね。
examplePolite.english: Preparing for Christmas already? You're getting ahead of yourself.

entry.notes: Also about yourself: chotto ki ga hayai kedo (it's early, but...).

literal: the moment of dying is bad

entry.kana: おうじょうぎわがわるい
entry.literal: the moment of dying is bad
entry.use: A tease for someone who keeps arguing a lost point, won't pay up on a bet or makes excuses when caught: mou, oujougiwa warui na. Narrower than akirame ga warui, which can be praise.

example.romaji: mou maketan da kara, oujougiwa warui yo.
example.ja: もう負けたんだから、往生際悪いよ。
example.english: You've already lost, just accept it.

examplePolite.romaji: mou maketan desu kara, oujougiwa ga warui desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: もう負けたんですから、往生際が悪いですよ。
examplePolite.english: You've already lost, so stop fighting it.

entry.notes: Oujou = passing away; people hear oujougiwa as one word.

entry.use: About spending or pretending beyond your means to look good, like a pricey date or a brand bag on credit: mie hatte takai mise ni shichatta, with o dropped. Iji o haru is pride that won't back down, not showing off.

example.romaji: mie hatte takai mise yoyaku shichatta.
example.ja: 見栄張って高い店予約しちゃった。
example.english: I showed off and booked a pricey place.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui mie o hatte, takai mise o yoyaku shichaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: つい見栄を張って、高い店を予約しちゃいました。
examplePolite.english: I wanted to look good, so I booked a pricey restaurant.

entry.notes: Noun: mieppari (a show-off, someone vain).

entry.use: Praise for a new hire, student or kid who picks up a task fast: nomikomi hayai ne! The opposite nomikomi ga osoi (slow to pick things up) is often said of yourself. It's about learning; atama no kaiten ga hayai is about thinking on your feet.

example.romaji: nomikomi hayai ne! mou oboeta no?
example.ja: 飲み込み早いね！もう覚えたの？
example.english: You're a quick learner! You've got it already?

examplePolite.romaji: nomikomi ga hayai desu ne! mou oboeta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 飲み込みが早いですね！もう覚えたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You pick things up fast! You've learned it already?

entry.notes: Opposite: nomikomi ga osoi (slow to pick things up).

entry.use: A jab at someone, often a man, who sulks or gets angry over something trivial, like splitting a bill to the yen: utsuwa chiisai naa. The opposite utsuwa ga ookii praises a big-hearted leader; kokoro ga semai is close.

example.romaji: sonna koto de okoru nante, utsuwa chiisai naa.
example.ja: そんなことで怒るなんて、器小さいなあ。
example.english: Getting angry over that? How petty.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna koto de okoru nante, utsuwa ga chiisai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そんなことで怒るなんて、器が小さいですね。
examplePolite.english: Getting angry over something like that is rather petty.

entry.notes: Opposite: utsuwa ga ookii (big-hearted, a natural leader).

entry.use: Warm concern for how a person is doing, heard most as thanks: itsumo ki ni kakete kurete arigatou (thanks for always looking out for me). Not ki ni suru (mind, worry about), which is fretting over a thing.

example.romaji: itsumo ki ni kakete kurete, arigatou ne.
example.ja: いつも気にかけてくれて、ありがとうね。
example.english: Thanks for always looking out for me.

examplePolite.romaji: itsumo ki ni kakete itadaite, arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: いつも気にかけていただいて、ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for always looking out for me.

entry.notes: Also for your own health: kenkou o ki ni kakeru (watch your health).

english: we all need help sometimes; you'd do the same for me

entry.english: we all need help sometimes; you'd do the same for me
entry.use: The reflex reply when a neighbour, colleague or friend thanks you or apologises for needing help: iie, otagaisama desu yo. It says the help runs both ways, so nobody owes anyone; the full line is komatta toki wa otagaisama.

example.romaji: ii tte, otagaisama da yo.
example.ja: いいって、お互い様だよ。
example.english: Don't mention it, you'd do the same for me.

examplePolite.romaji: iie, komatta toki wa otagaisama desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: いいえ、困ったときはお互い様ですから。
examplePolite.english: Not at all, we all need help sometimes.

entry.notes: Close: mochitsu motaretsu (give and take).

english: put yourself in the other person's place

entry.english: put yourself in the other person's place
entry.use: Advice from parents, teachers and friends, almost always aite no mi ni natte kangaete (think how they'd feel). Any person can stand in for aite: kodomo no mi ni natte. It's imagining one person's side; kuuki o yomu is sensing the room.

example.romaji: aite no mi ni natte kangaete mina yo.
example.ja: 相手の身になって考えてみなよ。
example.english: Try seeing it from their side.

examplePolite.romaji: aite no mi ni natte kangaete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 相手の身になって考えてみてください。
examplePolite.english: Please try to see it from their side.

entry.notes: Also aite no tachiba ni natte (from their position).

english: be a handful, need constant looking after

entry.english: be a handful, need constant looking after
entry.use: Fond grumbling about a child, partner, junior or pet who keeps needing help: mattaku, sewa ga yakeru na. There's affection in it; mendokusai is plain annoyance.

example.romaji: mattaku, sewa ga yakeru na.
example.ja: まったく、世話が焼けるな。
example.english: Honestly, you're such a handful.

examplePolite.romaji: uchi no musuko wa, hontou ni sewa ga yakeru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: うちの息子は、本当に世話が焼けるんです。
examplePolite.english: My son is such a handful.

entry.notes: sewa o yaku = fuss over someone; a born fusser is a sewayaki.

english: please, I'm begging you (just this once)

entry.kana: いっしょうのおねがい
entry.english: please, I'm begging you (just this once)
entry.use: The dramatic plea among friends and siblings, or from kids to parents, often with hands pressed together: isshou no onegai! Everyone uses it again and again despite the name, which is half the joke.

example.romaji: isshou no onegai! kondo dake okane kashite.
example.ja: 一生のお願い！今度だけお金貸して。
example.english: I'm begging you! Lend me some money just this once.

english: both as bad as each other

entry.english: both as bad as each other
entry.englishIdiom: six of one and half a dozen of the other
entry.use: The verdict on a quarrel or a couple's fight where neither side is innocent: sore wa dotchi mo dotchi da yo. Also for two equally poor choices. It refuses to take sides, unlike kata o motsu.

example.romaji: sore wa dotchi mo dotchi da yo.
example.ja: それはどっちもどっちだよ。
example.english: You're both as bad as each other.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa, dotchi mo dotchi desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これは、どっちもどっちですね。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, they're both as bad as each other.

english: lend your support, help (with something big)

entry.english: lend your support, help (with something big)
entry.use: The serious ask for backing on a project, a cause or a hard situation: chikara o kashite hoshii (I need your help). Bigger than te o kasu (a quick hand); chikara ni naru is offering support yourself.

example.romaji: kono purojekuto, chikara kashite kurenai?
example.ja: このプロジェクト、力貸してくれない？
example.english: Would you help me out on this project?

examplePolite.romaji: kono purojekuto ni, zehi chikara o kashite itadakemasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: このプロジェクトに、ぜひ力を貸していただけませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you be willing to help us with this project?

entry.notes: chie o kasu = help someone think something through.

entry.use: The rallying line for a team, class, family or workplace facing something hard, usually minna de chikara o awasete (all of us together). Heard in pep talks and speeches as much as in chat; te o kumu is two sides forming an alliance.

example.romaji: minna de chikara awasete ganbarou!
example.ja: みんなで力合わせて頑張ろう！
example.english: Let's all pull together!

examplePolite.romaji: minna de chikara o awasete ganbarimashou.
examplePolite.ja: みんなで力を合わせて頑張りましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's all pull together and do our best.

english: not my problem, I couldn't care less
literal: (it's) not a thing I know about

entry.english: not my problem, I couldn't care less
entry.literal: (it's) not a thing I know about
entry.use: A rough brush-off when someone's trouble lands on you: sonna no shitta kotcha nai (that's not my problem). Said in anger or bluster, more often by men; the milder version is kankei nai.

example.romaji: sonna no, ore no shitta kotcha nai yo.
example.ja: そんなの、俺の知ったこっちゃないよ。
example.english: That's not my problem.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: kankei nai (none of my business).

entry.use: About a shy child, a new colleague, a rescued pet or a guarded partner finally trusting you: yatto kokoro o hiraite kureta, or nakanaka kokoro o hirakanai. kyori o oku is the opposite move.

example.romaji: ano ko, yatto kokoro hiraite kureta.
example.ja: あの子、やっと心開いてくれた。
example.english: She's finally opened up to me.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko, yatto kokoro o hiraite kureta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの子、やっと心を開いてくれたんです。
examplePolite.english: She's finally opened up to me.

entry.notes: Close: kokoro o yurusu / ki o yurusu (trust someone, let your guard down).

english: try to get someone's attention (often romantic)

entry.english: try to get someone's attention (often romantic)
entry.use: Dating talk about playing for someone's interest: kare no ki o hikitakute (because I wanted his attention); also a child acting up to be noticed. It's the effort; ki ga aru is already being into someone, and myaku ga aru is them liking you back.

example.romaji: kare no ki o hikitakute, wazato sokkenaku shiteru no.
example.ja: 彼の気を引きたくて、わざとそっけなくしてるの。
example.english: I'm playing it cool on purpose to get his attention.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no ki o hikitakute, wazato sokkenaku shite iru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の気を引きたくて、わざとそっけなくしているんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm playing it cool on purpose to get his attention.

entry.notes: Not hiku on its own, slang for being put off (sore wa hiku).

english: cross the line; (of two people) sleep together

entry.english: cross the line; (of two people) sleep together
entry.use: Gossip about two people who've become lovers (ano futari, issen koeta rashii yo), or about going too far in a fight or a joke. The romantic sense is the one you'll hear most.

example.romaji: ano futari, mou issen koeta rashii yo.
example.ja: あの二人、もう一線越えたらしいよ。
example.english: Apparently those two have already slept together.

examplePolite.romaji: ano futari, mou issen o koeta rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの二人、もう一線を越えたらしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Apparently those two have already slept together.

entry.notes: issen o hiku = draw a line, keep a boundary.

english: go to a lot of trouble (for someone)

entry.english: go to a lot of trouble (for someone)
entry.use: Mostly in thanks for effort made on your behalf: iroiro hone otte kurete arigatou, or hone o otte itadaite at work. Also literally breaking a bone (ashi no hone o otta); hone ga oreru is a job being hard work.

example.romaji: iroiro hone otte kurete, arigatou.
example.ja: いろいろ骨折ってくれて、ありがとう。
example.english: Thanks for going to all that trouble.

examplePolite.romaji: iroiro to hone o otte itadaite, arigatou gozaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: いろいろと骨を折っていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you for going to so much trouble for us.

entry.notes: Noun: honeori (honeori zon = all that effort for nothing).

entry.use: Breaking off for good with family, an ex, a toxic friend or a gang, often oya to en o kitta or ano hito to wa mou en o kitta. Far stronger than kyori o oku (a break).

example.romaji: ano hito to wa mou en kitta kara.
example.ja: あの人とはもう縁切ったから。
example.english: I've cut ties with her.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito to wa, mou en o kirimashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの人とは、もう縁を切りました。
examplePolite.english: I've cut ties with her.

entry.notes: Also te o kiru (break off with a partner or associate).

english: I owe you big, I'm really grateful

entry.english: I owe you big, I'm really grateful
entry.use: A heartfelt, slightly old-school thank-you when someone bails you out, mostly men among friends: warui na, on ni kiru yo. kari ga aru describes the debt; this is the thanks you say on the spot.

example.romaji: warui na, on ni kiru yo.
example.ja: 悪いな、恩に着るよ。
example.english: Thanks, man. I owe you big.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni tasukarimashita. on ni kimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 本当に助かりました。恩に着ます。
examplePolite.english: You really saved me. I owe you big.

entry.notes: on o kaesu = repay a kindness; onkisegamashii = making a big show of a favour.

english: make an enemy of, get on someone's bad side

entry.english: make an enemy of, get on someone's bad side
entry.use: A warning about someone powerful or vindictive: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai yo. Also about taking on many at once (minna o teki ni mawashite mo); mikata ni tsukeru (win someone over) is the opposite.

example.romaji: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai yo.
example.ja: あの人を敵に回すと怖いよ。
example.english: You don't want to get on her bad side.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito o teki ni mawasu to kowai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの人を敵に回すと怖いですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't want to get on her bad side.

english: call it a night, wrap up (a party)

entry.english: call it a night, wrap up (a party)
entry.use: How a party, drinking session or wedding gets ended, since owaru is avoided at celebrations: jaa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shiyou ka. When telling what happened: ohiraki ni natta (it broke up).

example.romaji: jaa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shiyou ka.
example.ja: じゃあ、そろそろお開きにしようか。
example.english: OK, shall we call it a night?

examplePolite.romaji: sore de wa, sorosoro ohiraki ni shitai to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: それでは、そろそろお開きにしたいと思います。
examplePolite.english: Well, I think it's about time we wrapped up.

entry.use: A work and family complaint about fixing what someone else messed up: mata ore ga ano hito no shirinugui ka yo. Often shirinugui o saserareru (get stuck cleaning up); ashi o hipparu is the one making the mess.

example.romaji: mata ore ga ano hito no shirinugui ka yo.
example.ja: また俺があの人の尻拭いかよ。
example.english: So I'm cleaning up his mess again?

examplePolite.romaji: mata watashi ga ano hito no shirinugui o suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: また私があの人の尻拭いをするんですか？
examplePolite.english: So I'm cleaning up his mess again?

english: be meant to be, have a connection

entry.english: be meant to be, have a connection
entry.use: Heard most in the negative to soften a breakup, rejection or failed job hunt: en ga nakatta n da yo (it just wasn't meant to be). In business it's the polite goodbye mata goen ga areba (if our paths cross again).

example.romaji: kanojo to wa en ga nakatta n da yo.
example.ja: 彼女とは縁がなかったんだよ。
example.english: It just wasn't meant to be with her.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo to wa, en ga nakatta n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女とは、縁がなかったんですよ。
examplePolite.english: It just wasn't meant to be with her.

entry.notes: On a chance meeting: kore mo nanika no en (this must be fate).

english: put a damper on, spoil the mood

entry.english: put a damper on, spoil the mood
entry.use: Mostly the apology before bad news or an objection: mizu sasu you de warui kedo (sorry to be a downer, but). Also coming between a happy couple or friends (futari no naka ni mizu o sasu). Not mizu ni nagasu (forgive and forget).

example.romaji: mizu sasu you de warui kedo, sono hi ame rashii yo.
example.ja: 水差すようで悪いけど、その日雨らしいよ。
example.english: Sorry to be a downer, but it's supposed to rain that day.

examplePolite.romaji: mizu o sasu you de moushiwake nai n desu ga, sono hi wa ame rashii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 水を差すようで申し訳ないんですが、その日は雨らしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Sorry to be a downer, but it's supposed to rain that day.

english: just click with someone, get on well

entry.english: just click with someone, get on well
entry.use: The same as ki ga au, said of two people who get on naturally, often with a hint of surprise: buchou to wa fushigi to uma ga au. Common in the negative too (dou mo uma ga awanai). Don't hear it as umai (tasty, skilled).

example.romaji: buchou to wa, fushigi to uma ga au n da.
example.ja: 部長とは、不思議と馬が合うんだ。
example.english: Weirdly, I really click with my boss.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou to wa, fushigi to uma ga au n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 部長とは、不思議と馬が合うんです。
examplePolite.english: Weirdly, I really click with my boss.

entry.notes: From riding: horse and rider in step.

entry.use: A complaint about being the last to know or shut out of a decision: nande ore dake kaya no soto na no? Heard at work, among friends and in families, often as kaya no soto ni sareta (got shut out).

example.romaji: nande ore dake kaya no soto na no?
example.ja: なんで俺だけ蚊帳の外なの？
example.english: Why am I the only one left out?

examplePolite.romaji: watashi dake kaya no soto datta n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私だけ蚊帳の外だったんですね。
examplePolite.english: So I was the only one left out of the loop.

english: there's a chance (they like you back)

entry.english: there's a chance (they like you back)
entry.use: Dating talk reading someone's signals, nearly always as myaku ari (promising) or myaku nashi (no chance): sore, myaku ari da yo. The literal 'there's a pulse' is medical; ki ga aru is someone actually being into you.

example.romaji: henji sugu kuru n desho? sore, myaku ari da yo.
example.ja: 返事すぐ来るんでしょ？それ、脈ありだよ。
example.english: He texts back right away? You've got a shot.

examplePolite.romaji: henji ga hayai nara, myaku ari desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 返事が早いなら、脈ありですよ。
examplePolite.english: If he replies fast, you've got a shot.

entry.notes: Usually myaku ari / myaku nashi.

english: (negative) disapprove; play nice to please people

entry.english: (negative) disapprove; play nice to please people
entry.use: Two everyday uses. The negative ii kao o shinai is parents or a boss not approving (oya ga ii kao shinai). The positive is being nice to keep people happy, often dare ni demo ii kao suru (a people-pleaser). Don't confuse it with kao ga ii (good-looking).

example.romaji: oya ga ii kao shinai n da yo ne, kare no koto.
example.ja: 親がいい顔しないんだよね、彼のこと。
example.english: My parents aren't too happy about him.

examplePolite.romaji: ryoushin ga, amari ii kao o shinai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 両親が、あまりいい顔をしないんですよね。
examplePolite.english: My parents aren't too happy about it.

entry.notes: A people-pleaser: dare ni demo ii kao suru hito (happou bijin).

english: owe someone too much to stand up to them

entry.english: owe someone too much to stand up to them
entry.use: About a wife, older sibling, mentor or boss who's done so much for you that you can never argue back: ane ni wa atama ga agaranai. Always negative and said with fond resignation; shiri ni shikareru is being bossed around without the gratitude.

example.romaji: ane ni wa atama ga agaranai n da yo.
example.ja: 姉には頭が上がらないんだよ。
example.english: I owe my sister too much to ever argue with her.

examplePolite.romaji: ane ni wa, hontou ni atama ga agarimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 姉には、本当に頭が上がりません。
examplePolite.english: I owe my sister so much, I can never argue with her.

entry.use: Mostly a complaint about someone always checking how a boss, parent or partner will react: joushi no kaoiro bakkari ukagatteru. Close to kuuki o yomu, but fixed on one person's mood and the fear of upsetting them.

example.romaji: ano hito, itsumo joushi no kaoiro bakkari ukagatteru.
example.ja: あの人、いつも上司の顔色ばっかりうかがってる。
example.english: He's always tiptoeing around the boss.

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito, itsumo joushi no kaoiro bakari ukagattemasu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの人、いつも上司の顔色ばかりうかがってますよね。
examplePolite.english: He's always tiptoeing around the boss, isn't he?

entry.notes: Literal kaoiro ga warui = look pale.

entry.use: Said before janken, a draw, a bet or a vote so the loser won't sulk: uramikko nashi ne. Also after the result, to keep things friendly.

example.romaji: janken de kimeyou. uramikko nashi ne.
example.ja: じゃんけんで決めよう。恨みっこなしね。
example.english: Let's settle it with rock-paper-scissors. No hard feelings.

examplePolite.romaji: dou natte mo, uramikko nashi desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: どうなっても、恨みっこなしですよ。
examplePolite.english: Whatever happens, no hard feelings.

english: let someone save face, defer to them

entry.english: let someone save face, defer to them
entry.use: Going along with a senior, a host or whoever introduced you so they don't look bad: koko wa senpai no kao o tatete. Often the reason you accept something you'd rather refuse; kao o tsubusu is the opposite.

example.romaji: koko wa senpai no kao o tatete, damatte okou.
example.ja: ここは先輩の顔を立てて、黙っておこう。
example.english: Let's keep quiet and let our senior save face.

examplePolite.romaji: koko wa senpai no kao o tatete, damatte okimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ここは先輩の顔を立てて、黙っておきましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's keep quiet and let our senior save face.

entry.use: Said to a friend, partner or relative who's being too polite or reserved with you: tanin gyougi da na (why so formal?). Often about keigo, over-thanking or refusing help; aka no tanin is an actual stranger.

example.romaji: keigo nante tanin gyougi da yo. futsuu ni hanashite.
example.ja: 敬語なんて他人行儀だよ。普通に話して。
example.english: Keigo feels so distant. Just talk normally.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna tanin gyougi na koto iwanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな他人行儀なこと言わないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't be so formal with me.

english: make someone (who vouched for you) look bad

entry.english: make someone (who vouched for you) look bad
entry.use: A warning to someone you introduced or recommended: ore no kao, tsubusanaide yo (don't embarrass me). Also the complaint ore no kao o tsubushita; kao o tateru is the opposite.

example.romaji: shoukai shita ore no kao, tsubusanaide yo.
example.ja: 紹介した俺の顔、潰さないでよ。
example.english: I introduced you, so don't make me look bad.

examplePolite.romaji: shoukai shita watashi no kao o tsubusanaide kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 紹介した私の顔を潰さないでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: I introduced you, so please don't make me look bad.

entry.notes: Stronger: kao ni doro o nuru (oya no kao ni doro o nuru = disgrace your parents).

entry.englishIdiom: birds of a feather flock together
entry.use: A wry comment when a group turns out to share the same quirk or vice: rui wa tomo o yobu tte yatsu da ne. Can be teasing or a dig.

example.romaji: ano guruupu, minna nonbee da ne. rui wa tomo o yobu tte yatsu da.
example.ja: あのグループ、みんな飲兵衛だね。類は友を呼ぶってやつだ。
example.english: That whole group are big drinkers. Birds of a feather.

examplePolite.romaji: ano guruupu, minna osake ga suki desu ne. rui wa tomo o yobu tte yatsu desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あのグループ、みんなお酒が好きですね。類は友を呼ぶってやつですね。
examplePolite.english: That whole group loves a drink. Birds of a feather.

entry.notes: Short form: ruitomo.

entry.use: The worry behind every soft refusal or bit of feedback, usually kado ga tatanai you ni (so there's no bad feeling) or sonna iikata shitara kado ga tatsu. It's the wording or act causing friction; ki ni sawaru is how the other person takes it.

example.romaji: sonna iikata shitara, kado ga tatsu yo.
example.ja: そんな言い方したら、角が立つよ。
example.english: Saying it like that will rub people the wrong way.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna iikata o shitara, kado ga tachimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな言い方をしたら、角が立ちますよ。
examplePolite.english: Saying it like that will rub people the wrong way.

entry.notes: Opposite: maruku osamaru (be settled smoothly).

romaji: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii
english: the more you fight, the closer you are
literal: close to the point of fighting

entry.romaji: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii
entry.ja: 喧嘩するほど仲がいい
entry.kana: けんかするほどなかがいい
entry.english: the more you fight, the closer you are
entry.literal: close to the point of fighting
entry.use: Said about a bickering couple, siblings or friends, half teasing: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iu shi ne. Also a consolation after you've argued with someone you love.

example.romaji: mata kenka shiteru no? maa, kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iu shi ne.
example.ja: また喧嘩してるの？まあ、喧嘩するほど仲がいいって言うしね。
example.english: Fighting again? Well, they say the more you fight, the closer you are.

examplePolite.romaji: kenka suru hodo naka ga ii tte iimasu kara ne.
examplePolite.ja: 喧嘩するほど仲がいいって言いますからね。
examplePolite.english: They do say the more you fight, the closer you are.

romaji: yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi
english: other families do as they like; we do it our way
literal: elsewhere is elsewhere, home is home

entry.romaji: yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi
entry.ja: よそはよそ、うちはうち
entry.kana: よそはよそ、うちはうち
entry.english: other families do as they like; we do it our way
entry.literal: elsewhere is elsewhere, home is home
entry.use: Every parent's reply to 'but everyone else has one / is allowed': yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi. Also more widely, that other people's choices aren't yours to copy.

example.romaji: minna motteru tte? yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi desho.
example.ja: みんな持ってるって？よそはよそ、うちはうちでしょ。
example.english: Everyone has one? Other families can do what they like; this is our house.

examplePolite.romaji: yoso wa yoso, uchi wa uchi desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: よそはよそ、うちはうちですから。
examplePolite.english: Other places do things their way; we do ours.

literal: split the belly open and talk

entry.literal: split the belly open and talk
entry.use: An invitation to drop the politeness and say what you really think, usually as hara watte hanasou (let's talk honestly) between friends, partners or colleagues after some friction. The hara (belly) is where your true intentions are kept.

example.romaji: ikkai, hara o watte hanasou yo.
example.ja: 一回、腹を割って話そうよ。
example.english: Let's have a proper heart-to-heart.

examplePolite.romaji: ichido, hara o watte hanashimasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一度、腹を割って話しませんか？
examplePolite.english: Why don't we talk frankly, just this once?

entry.notes: Casual speech drops the o: hara watte hanasou.

english: settle it by talking to someone, sort it out with them

entry.english: settle it by talking to someone, sort it out with them
entry.use: Going to someone, often the other side or the person in charge, and settling a problem or getting their OK by talking: ore ga hanashi tsukete kuru (I'll go sort it out with them). Crime dramas give it a hint of muscle, but everyday use is just arranging things.

example.romaji: ooya-san ni wa watashi ga hanashi tsuketoku ne.
example.ja: 大家さんには私が話つけとくね。
example.english: I'll sort it out with the landlord.

examplePolite.romaji: ooya-san ni wa watashi kara hanashi o tsukete okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 大家さんには私から話をつけておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll get it settled with the landlord myself.

entry.notes: Once settled: hanashi ga tsuita (it's been sorted out).

english: reach someone's ears, get word of

entry.english: reach someone's ears, get word of
entry.use: News or a rumour reaching someone, often someone it shouldn't: buchou no mimi ni haittara yabai (if this gets to the boss, we're in trouble). Unlike mimi ni suru, the news is the subject; you just end up knowing. In the negative it can also mean you can't take in what's said: hanashi ga zenzen mimi ni hairanai.

example.romaji: sono uwasa, mou mimi ni haitteru yo.
example.ja: その噂、もう耳に入ってるよ。
example.english: That rumour's already reached me.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ken wa mou buchou no mimi ni haitte imasu.
examplePolite.ja: その件はもう部長の耳に入っています。
examplePolite.english: The manager has already heard about that.

english: just a figure of speech, not meant literally

entry.english: just a figure of speech, not meant literally
entry.use: The standard backpedal when someone takes your words too literally or too hard: ima no wa kotoba no aya da yo (that was just a way of putting it). Aya is the pattern woven into cloth.

example.romaji: gomen, ima no wa kotoba no aya da yo.
example.ja: ごめん、今のは言葉のあやだよ。
example.english: Sorry, that was just a figure of speech.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, ima no wa kotoba no aya desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、今のは言葉のあやです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I didn't mean that literally.

english: don't say such ominous things, don't jinx it

entry.english: don't say such ominous things, don't jinx it
entry.use: The quick rebuke when someone mentions death, illness, an accident or failure, even as a joke: engi demo nai koto iwanaide (don't say things like that). Engi is luck or omen, as in engi ga ii / engi ga warui.

example.romaji: chotto, engi demo nai koto iwanaide yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、縁起でもないこと言わないでよ。
example.english: Hey, bite your tongue! Don't say things like that.

examplePolite.romaji: engi demo nai koto iwanaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 縁起でもないこと言わないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't say such ominous things.

english: play dumb, pretend not to know

entry.english: play dumb, pretend not to know
entry.use: Accusing someone of pretending not to know what you mean when they clearly do: shira kitte mo muda da yo (no use playing dumb). Mostly said to someone else, as shira o kiru na or shira kiranaide. Finally telling under pressure is the opposite, kuchi o waru.

example.romaji: shira kitte mo muda da yo, miteta n da kara.
example.ja: しら切っても無駄だよ、見てたんだから。
example.english: No use playing dumb, I saw you.

examplePolite.romaji: shira o kitte mo muda desu yo, mite ita n desu kara.
examplePolite.ja: しらを切っても無駄ですよ、見ていたんですから。
examplePolite.english: There's no point pretending, I saw everything.

entry.notes: Single-word alternative: shirabakkureru.

english: can't fill the silence, run out of things to say
literal: the pause can't be held up

entry.english: can't fill the silence, run out of things to say
entry.literal: the pause can't be held up
entry.use: Said of a silence you can't fill: on a first date, in a lift with your boss, at a table where nobody talks. Usually about yourself or a situation, as futarikiri da to ma ga motanai (just the two of us, I run out of things to say). Also about killing time: sumaho ga nai to ma ga motanai.

example.romaji: futarikiri da to ma ga motanai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 二人きりだと間が持たないんだよね。
example.english: When it's just the two of us, I run out of things to say.

examplePolite.romaji: futarikiri da to ma ga motanai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 二人きりだと間が持たないんですよね。
examplePolite.english: When it's just the two of us, I never know how to fill the silence.

english: talk big, brag about what you'll do

entry.english: talk big, brag about what you'll do
entry.use: Bragging about what you can or will do, usually as a put-down or a warning: ooguchi tataku na (stop talking big). It's about the boast itself; kuchi dake is about never following through.

example.romaji: ooguchi tataku no wa katte kara ni shite.
example.ja: 大口叩くのは勝ってからにして。
example.english: Save the big talk for after you win.

examplePolite.romaji: ooguchi o tataku no wa katte kara ni shite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 大口を叩くのは勝ってからにしてください。
examplePolite.english: Please save the big talk until you've actually won.

entry.notes: Casual variant: dekai kuchi o tataku.

english: you've got some nerve (a sarcastic warning)

entry.english: you've got some nerve (a sarcastic warning)
entry.use: A sarcastic warning to someone who has just done or said something bold or cheeky, half-joking among friends or mock-threatening from a senior. Unlike yoku iu yo, which calls out hypocrisy, it's about daring to do something.

example.romaji: watashi no purin tabeta no? ii dokyou shiteru ja nai.
example.ja: 私のプリン食べたの？いい度胸してるじゃない。
example.english: You ate my pudding? You've got some nerve.

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no purin, tabemashita? ii dokyou shitemasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 私のプリン、食べました？いい度胸してますね。
examplePolite.english: You ate my pudding? You've got some nerve.

entry.notes: Also: ii dokyou da ne.

english: keep a secret to the grave
literal: carry it as far as the graveyard

entry.kana: はかばまでもっていく
entry.politeJa: 墓場まで持っていきます
entry.english: keep a secret to the grave
entry.literal: carry it as far as the graveyard
entry.use: Promising never to tell anyone, as a solemn vow or half-jokingly about something embarrassing: kono koto wa hakaba made motte iku (I'm taking this to the grave).

example.romaji: kono hanashi wa hakaba made motte iku yo.
example.ja: この話は墓場まで持っていくよ。
example.english: I'm taking this one to the grave.

examplePolite.romaji: kono hanashi wa hakaba made motte ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: この話は墓場まで持っていきますよ。
examplePolite.english: I'll take this one to the grave.

entry.notes: Also: haka made motte iku.

english: happen to hear, catch wind of
literal: tuck it into a little ear

entry.english: happen to hear, catch wind of
entry.literal: tuck it into a little ear
entry.use: Almost always in the past as a gossip opener: komimi ni hasanda n da kedo... (I happened to hear that...). It signals you heard it in passing and aren't sure it's true, which is softer than saying who told you.

example.romaji: komimi ni hasanda n da kedo, tanaka-san yameru no?
example.ja: 小耳に挟んだんだけど、田中さん辞めるの？
example.english: I happened to hear something. Is Tanaka quitting?

examplePolite.romaji: komimi ni hasanda n desu kedo, tanaka-san, yamerareru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 小耳に挟んだんですけど、田中さん、辞められるんですか？
examplePolite.english: I happened to hear something. Is Ms Tanaka leaving?

romaji: kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu
literal: say things that aren't even in your heart

entry.romaji: kokoro ni mo nai koto o iu
entry.polite: kokoro ni mo nai koto o iimasu
entry.ja: 心にもないことを言う
entry.kana: こころにもないことをいう
entry.politeJa: 心にもないことを言います
entry.literal: say things that aren't even in your heart
entry.use: Mostly in apologies after a fight: kokoro ni mo nai koto itchatta (I said things I didn't mean). The phrase kokoro ni mo nai also goes with flattery you don't mean: kokoro ni mo nai oseji.

example.romaji: tsui katto natte, kokoro ni mo nai koto itchatta.
example.ja: ついカッとなって、心にもないこと言っちゃった。
example.english: I lost my temper and said things I didn't mean.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui katto natte, kokoro ni mo nai koto o itte shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: ついカッとなって、心にもないことを言ってしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I lost my temper and said something I didn't mean.

english: hit a sore spot, say exactly the wrong thing

entry.english: hit a sore spot, say exactly the wrong thing
entry.use: Modern casual talk for accidentally bringing up the one topic that upsets someone, like an ex, their weight or their exam results: a, jirai funda (oops, touched a nerve). A person's jirai is their sore subject.

example.romaji: a, ima jirai funda kamo.
example.ja: あ、今地雷踏んだかも。
example.english: Oops, I think I just touched a nerve.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, jirai o funde shimatta mitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、地雷を踏んでしまったみたいです。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, it seems I touched a sore spot.

english: I'm not following, where is this going?

entry.english: I'm not following, where is this going?
entry.use: Said when you can't work out what someone is getting at or what it has to do with you: gomen, hanashi ga mienai n da kedo (sorry, I'm not following). It's about the point, not the words; not understanding the words is imi ga wakaranai.

example.romaji: gomen, hanashi ga mienai n da kedo.
example.ja: ごめん、話が見えないんだけど。
example.english: Sorry, I'm not following.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, chotto hanashi ga mienai n desu ga.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと話が見えないんですが。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'm not quite following.

entry.use: Mostly negative, about someone who won't say what they know: nakanaka kuchi o waranai (just won't spill). Crime dramas use it for suspects; in daily life it's said jokingly about friends hiding a crush or kids hiding mischief. Letting something slip by accident is kuchi ga suberu.

example.romaji: kanojo, nakanaka kuchi o waranai n da yo ne.
example.ja: 彼女、なかなか口を割らないんだよね。
example.english: She just won't spill.

examplePolite.romaji: musuko ga nakanaka kuchi o waranai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 息子がなかなか口を割らないんです。
examplePolite.english: My son just won't own up.

entry.use: Going along with what someone says so as not to spoil the mood or blow a cover: tekitou ni hanashi awaseteta (I was just nodding along), or as a request: hanashi awasete ne (back me up, OK?). Really getting on in conversation is hanashi ga au.

example.romaji: kare no mae de wa, hanashi awasete ne.
example.ja: 彼の前では、話合わせてね。
example.english: In front of him, just play along, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: kare no mae de wa, hanashi o awasete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の前では、話を合わせてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: When he's around, please play along.

entry.use: A good-humoured concession when someone outwits you with a clever reply or trick: kore wa ippon torareta na (well, you got me there). It's a fixed passive past; the ippon is a winning point in kendo or judo.

example.romaji: naruhodo ne, kore wa ippon torareta.
example.ja: なるほどね、これは一本取られた。
example.english: Ha, fair enough. You got me there.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, kore wa ippon toraremashita ne.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、これは一本取られましたね。
examplePolite.english: I see. You've got me there.

english: it's all in how you put it
literal: things depend on the way of saying

entry.english: it's all in how you put it
entry.literal: things depend on the way of saying
entry.use: A wry comment when someone dresses up something bad in nice words, or a reminder that the same thing can be said kindly or harshly: koseiteki tte, mono wa iiyou da ne ('unique'? nice way to put it). Also mono mo iiyou.

example.romaji: koseiteki tte, mono wa iiyou da ne.
example.ja: 個性的って、物は言いようだね。
example.english: 'Unique'? That's one way to put it.

examplePolite.romaji: koseiteki tte, mono wa iiyou desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 個性的って、物は言いようですね。
examplePolite.english: 'Unique'? That's a nice way of putting it.

entry.notes: Full saying: mono mo iiyou de kado ga tatsu (how you say it decides whether it offends).

english: don't be silly, don't talk nonsense

entry.politeJa: バカなこと言わないでください
entry.english: don't be silly, don't talk nonsense
entry.use: Brushes off a ridiculous idea, or reassures someone who is putting themselves down: baka iwanaide, sonna wake nai desho (don't be silly, of course not). The rougher, mostly male form is baka iu na. In polite speech it becomes baka na koto iwanaide kudasai, which is still quite direct.

example.romaji: baka iwanaide, sonna wake nai desho.
example.ja: バカ言わないで、そんなわけないでしょ。
example.english: Don't be silly, of course not.

examplePolite.romaji: baka na koto iwanaide kudasai yo, sonna wake nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: バカなこと言わないでくださいよ、そんなわけないですよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't be silly, that's not true at all.

entry.notes: Rougher: baka iu na; baka ie (yeah, right).

english: interrupt and derail what someone is saying
literal: break the waist of the talk

entry.english: interrupt and derail what someone is saying
entry.literal: break the waist of the talk
entry.use: Cutting in so the speaker loses their thread, as a complaint (hanashi no koshi oranaide) or an apology (hanashi no koshi o otte gomen). kuchi o hasamu is chiming in; this is derailing what someone was in the middle of saying.

example.romaji: chotto, hanashi no koshi oranaide yo.
example.ja: ちょっと、話の腰折らないでよ。
example.english: Hey, don't cut me off.

examplePolite.romaji: hanashi no koshi o otte sumimasen ga, hitotsu dake ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 話の腰を折ってすみませんが、一つだけいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry to interrupt, but may I add just one thing?

literal: stick a bad omen on it

entry.literal: stick a bad omen on it
entry.use: Criticising or nitpicking something, often unfairly or out of spite: nan ni demo kechi tsukeru (finds fault with everything). The kechi here is an old word for a bad omen, not kechi (stingy).

example.romaji: hito no ryouri ni kechi tsukenaide yo.
example.ja: 人の料理にケチつけないでよ。
example.english: Don't knock my cooking.

examplePolite.romaji: hito no ryouri ni kechi o tsukenaide kudasai yo.
examplePolite.ja: 人の料理にケチをつけないでくださいよ。
examplePolite.english: Please don't criticise my cooking.

entry.polite: ne mo ha mo nai desu
entry.use: Almost always before uwasa (rumour): ne mo ha mo nai uwasa (a groundless rumour). It's the fixed way to deny gossip about yourself or someone else; makka na uso is a flat lie, this is talk with nothing behind it.

example.romaji: sonna no, ne mo ha mo nai uwasa da yo.
example.ja: そんなの、根も葉もない噂だよ。
example.english: That's a totally groundless rumour.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ne mo ha mo nai uwasa desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それは根も葉もない噂ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That rumour has no basis at all.

english: would never say it, not in a million years
literal: can't say it even if my mouth tears open

entry.ja: 口が裂けても言えない
entry.kana: くちがさけてもいえない
entry.politeJa: 口が裂けても言えません
entry.english: would never say it, not in a million years
entry.literal: can't say it even if my mouth tears open
entry.use: An emphatic refusal to say something, either a secret or something too embarrassing or proud to admit: kare ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo ienai (I could never tell him). Also kuchi ga sakete mo iwanai (I'll never tell).

example.romaji: honnin ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo ienai yo.
example.ja: 本人には口が裂けても言えないよ。
example.english: I'd never tell her that, not in a million years.

examplePolite.romaji: honnin ni wa kuchi ga sakete mo iemasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 本人には口が裂けても言えませんよ。
examplePolite.english: I could never say that to her, not ever.

entry.use: A slightly more formal kuchi ni dasu, used for words and names: sono namae, nido to kuchi ni suru na (never mention that name again). It also means eating or drinking: kyou wa mada nani mo kuchi ni shite nai (I haven't had a thing today). It's the mouth twin of mimi ni suru.

example.romaji: sore, ano hito no mae de kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: それ、あの人の前で口にしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Better not mention that in front of him.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa ano kata no mae de kuchi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: それはあの方の前で口にしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to mention that in front of her.

entry.use: Shock at news or at something someone said, almost always in the past: kiita toki, mimi o utagatta yo (when I heard, I couldn't believe my ears). Also jibun no mimi o utagau.

example.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, mimi o utagatta yo.
example.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、耳を疑ったよ。
example.english: When I heard he was getting married, I couldn't believe my ears.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, mimi o utagaimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、耳を疑いましたよ。
examplePolite.english: When I heard he was getting married, I couldn't believe my ears.

entry.use: Mostly in the negative about work you haven't started, as X ni te o tsukeru: mada zenzen te o tsukete nai, doko kara te o tsukereba ii ka wakaranai (don't know where to start). It also means leaving food or money untouched (chokin ni wa te o tsukenai); in speech the o often drops.

example.romaji: repooto, mada zenzen te tsuketenai
example.ja: レポート、まだ全然手つけてない
example.english: I haven't even started on the report.

examplePolite.romaji: repooto ni wa mada zenzen te o tsukete inai n desu
examplePolite.ja: レポートにはまだ全然手をつけていないんです
examplePolite.english: I haven't even started on the report.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: hajimeru (start).

entry.use: Said when a problem has beaten you and there's nothing more you can do, usually as mou oteage (da): a broken computer, homework, a stubborn person, a hopeless situation. It is giving up on solving something, not quitting a task.

example.romaji: kore wa mou oteage da yo
example.ja: これはもうお手上げだよ
example.english: I give up on this one.

examplePolite.romaji: kore wa mou oteage desu
examplePolite.ja: これはもうお手上げです
examplePolite.english: I give up on this one.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: mou muri.

english: can't keep this up, it'll wear me out

entry.english: can't keep this up, it'll wear me out
entry.use: The standard complaint about overtime, late nights, drinking or training you can't sustain, often after konna ... ja or a -tara clause: konna peesu ja karada ga motanai. The ga often drops, and mi ga motanai means the same.

example.romaji: konna ni zangyou tsuzuitara karada motanai yo
example.ja: こんなに残業続いたら体もたないよ
example.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

examplePolite.romaji: konna ni zangyou ga tsuzuitara karada ga motanai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: こんなに残業が続いたら体がもたないですよ
examplePolite.english: If all this overtime keeps up, I won't last.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: mou genkai (I'm at my limit).

english: get the knack, work out how to do it

entry.english: get the knack, work out how to do it
entry.use: Said whenever a skill, sport, game or job starts to click: yatto kotsu tsukanda! The o usually drops; kotsu ga wakaru means much the same, and kotsu alone is the trick to something (kotsu o oshiete, tell me the trick).

example.romaji: yatto kotsu tsukanda kamo
example.ja: やっとコツつかんだかも
example.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

examplePolite.romaji: yatto kotsu o tsukanda ki ga shimasu
examplePolite.ja: やっとコツをつかんだ気がします
examplePolite.english: I think I've finally got the hang of it.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: nareru (get used to it).

entry.use: The cheerful yes when someone asks you a favour, said by the helper about the favour: oyasui goyou da yo. Not asameshi mae, which is boasting that a task is easy for you.

example.romaji: oyasui goyou da yo, makasete
example.ja: お安い御用だよ、任せて
example.english: No problem, leave it to me.

examplePolite.romaji: oyasui goyou desu yo, makasete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: お安い御用ですよ、任せてください
examplePolite.english: No problem, leave it to me.

entry.notes: Plainer: ii yo, makasete (sure, leave it to me).

english: be no match for, can't compete

entry.english: be no match for, can't compete
entry.use: Said of a pro, a rival or a big competitor you can't hope to match, usually as X ni wa tachiuchi dekinai: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai, ookii mise no nedan ni wa tachiuchi dekinai. Close to ha ga tatanai, which leans more to a fight or a problem you can't crack.

example.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekinai yo
example.ja: プロには太刀打ちできないよ
example.english: There's no competing with a pro.

examplePolite.romaji: puro ni wa tachiuchi dekimasen yo
examplePolite.ja: プロには太刀打ちできませんよ
examplePolite.english: There's no competing with a pro.

entry.use: Asking or saying whether someone is free to help right now: te aiteru? (got a sec?), te ga aitara onegai (when you're free). The opposite of te ga hanasenai; it is a free moment at work or home, not a free day.

example.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte
example.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝って
example.english: When you've got a free moment, give me a hand.

examplePolite.romaji: te ga aitara chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka
examplePolite.ja: 手が空いたらちょっと手伝ってもらえますか
examplePolite.english: When you've got a free moment, could you give me a hand?

entry.notes: Plain alternative: hima (hima? = are you free?).

english: be distracted by, too caught up in

entry.english: be distracted by, too caught up in
entry.use: Explaining a slip: you were caught up in one thing (X ni ki o torarete) and missed or forgot something else, as in sumaho ni ki o torarete norisugoshita. Ki ga chiru is losing focus to noise or interruptions; ki o torareru names the one thing that took your attention.

example.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshichatta.
example.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしちゃった。
example.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

examplePolite.romaji: sumaho ni ki o torarete, norisugoshite shimaimashita.
examplePolite.ja: スマホに気を取られて、乗り過ごしてしまいました。
examplePolite.english: I was so caught up in my phone I missed my stop.

english: can think of nothing else, preoccupied

entry.english: can think of nothing else, preoccupied
entry.use: Said as X no koto de atama ga ippai: an exam, a crush, money or a sick parent fills your head and leaves no room for anything else. Shika atama ni nai is the teasing version about someone else.

example.romaji: ima wa shiken no koto de atama ga ippai.
example.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱい。
example.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.
