examplePolite.ja: 今は試験のことで頭がいっぱいなんです。
examplePolite.english: Right now the exam is all I can think about.

entry.notes: Overwhelmed: atama ga ippai ippai (can't take any more in).

romaji: nani ga nan da ka wakaranai
english: have no idea what's going on

entry.romaji: nani ga nan da ka wakaranai
entry.polite: nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen
entry.ja: 何が何だか分からない
entry.kana: なにがなんだかわからない
entry.politeJa: 何が何だか分かりません
entry.english: have no idea what's going on
entry.use: Said when too much happens at once or something comes out of nowhere and you're lost. It's often cut short to nani ga nan da ka. Wake ga wakaranai judges something as absurd; this one is just being lost.

example.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakannai yo.
example.ja: 急にそんなこと言われても、何が何だか分かんないよ。
example.english: You spring that on me and I've no idea what's going on.

examplePolite.romaji: kyuu ni sonna koto o iwarete mo, nani ga nan da ka wakarimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: 急にそんなことを言われても、何が何だか分かりませんよ。
examplePolite.english: You spring that on me and I've no idea what's going on.

entry.notes: Casual: nani ga nan da ka wakannai, or just nani ga nan da ka.

entry.use: For a scene or reaction you can already see in your mind, usually someone's face: okaasan no okoru kao ga me ni ukabu. Atama ni ukabu is an idea or word popping up; me ni ukabu is a picture.

example.romaji: kanojo no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabu yo.
example.ja: 彼女の喜ぶ顔が目に浮かぶよ。
example.english: I can just picture how happy she'll be.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo no yorokobu kao ga me ni ukabimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女の喜ぶ顔が目に浮かびますね。
examplePolite.english: I can just picture how happy she'll be.

entry.use: Said of someone who nods along but isn't listening, often because they're in love or worried: sakki kara uwa no sora da yo. It works like a na-adjective: uwa no sora de kiku (half listen).

example.romaji: nee, kiiteru? sakki kara uwa no sora da yo.
example.ja: ねえ、聞いてる？さっきから上の空だよ。
example.english: Hey, are you listening? You've been miles away.

examplePolite.romaji: anou, kiite imasu ka? sakki kara uwa no sora desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの、聞いていますか？さっきから上の空ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Um, are you listening? You've been miles away.

entry.use: A slightly wry, old-style way to say someone's mind is elsewhere, usually from love or worry, said as a block with da or tte kanji. Arazu is old Japanese for nai. Uwa no sora is the everyday version.

example.romaji: kyou no kare, kokoro koko ni arazu tte kanji.
example.ja: 今日の彼、心ここにあらずって感じ。
example.english: He's totally somewhere else today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no kare wa kokoro koko ni arazu tte kanji desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 今日の彼は心ここにあらずって感じですね。
examplePolite.english: He's totally somewhere else today.

entry.use: Said when worry or excitement leaves you unable to get anything done, with the task as the subject: shinpai de shigoto ga te ni tsukanai. It's almost always negative. Ki ga chiru is distraction from outside; this one comes from inside.

example.romaji: shinpai de, shigoto ga zenzen te ni tsukanai.
example.ja: 心配で、仕事が全然手につかない。
example.english: I'm too worried to get any work done.

examplePolite.romaji: shinpai de, shigoto ga zenzen te ni tsukimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 心配で、仕事が全然手につきません。
examplePolite.english: I'm too worried to get any work done.

entry.notes: Close: mi ga hairanai (can't put your heart into it).

entry.use: About information: rumours, something online, what an expert or a salesperson says. It's mostly advice in the negative: unomi ni shinai hou ga ii. Ma ni ukeru is believing a joke or a line that wasn't meant seriously.

example.romaji: netto no uwasa, unomi ni shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: ネットの噂、鵜呑みにしないほうがいいよ。
example.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

examplePolite.romaji: netto no uwasa wa unomi ni shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ネットの噂は鵜呑みにしないほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Don't believe every rumour you read online.

english: only half believe what you hear

entry.kana: はなしはんぶんにきく
entry.english: only half believe what you hear
entry.englishIdiom: take it with a pinch of salt
entry.use: Advice about someone who exaggerates, or about boasts, gossip and sales talk; you'll mostly hear it as hanashi hanbun ni kiite oku. Unomi ni suru is the opposite: swallowing it all.

example.romaji: kare no hanashi, hanashi hanbun ni kiitoita hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 彼の話、話半分に聞いといたほうがいいよ。
example.english: Take what he says with a pinch of salt.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no hanashi wa, hanashi hanbun ni kiite oita hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の話は、話半分に聞いておいたほうがいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: Take what he says with a pinch of salt.

entry.use: Said about how you felt at first about news, a rumour or a too-good offer, usually in the past: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta. It works like a na-adjective: hanshin hangi de kiku.

example.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi datta kedo, hontou datta.
example.ja: 最初は半信半疑だったけど、本当だった。
example.english: I only half believed it at first, but it was true.

examplePolite.romaji: saisho wa hanshin hangi deshita kedo, hontou deshita.
examplePolite.ja: 最初は半信半疑でしたけど、本当でした。
examplePolite.english: I only half believed it at first, but it was true.

entry.use: Said defensively when someone warns you about a risk or downside you've already weighed, often followed by but: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi da kedo...

example.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi da yo. demo yaru.
example.ja: 危ないのは百も承知だよ。でもやる。
example.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

examplePolite.romaji: abunai no wa hyaku mo shouchi desu. demo yarimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 危ないのは百も承知です。でもやります。
examplePolite.english: I know full well it's risky. I'm doing it anyway.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: wakatteru tte (I know, I know).

english: never did it, know nothing about it
literal: no memory of it in oneself

entry.politeJa: 身に覚えがありません
entry.english: never did it, know nothing about it
entry.literal: no memory of it in oneself
entry.use: The standard denial when you're blamed or billed for something you didn't do: zenzen mi ni oboe ga nai. You'll also hear it about unknown charges, mi ni oboe no nai seikyuu. Kokoroatari ga nai is having no idea about a cause; this one denies your own part.

example.romaji: e, watashi ga? zenzen mi ni oboe nai n da kedo.
example.ja: え、私が？全然身に覚えないんだけど。
example.english: Me? I never did anything like that.

examplePolite.romaji: e, watashi ga desu ka? zenzen mi ni oboe ga nai n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: え、私がですか？全然身に覚えがないんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Me? I never did anything like that.

literal: nothing but X is in the head

entry.literal: nothing but X is in the head
entry.use: A complaint or tease about someone obsessed: X no koto shika atama ni nai (all he thinks about is X). Without shika, atama ni nakatta means it never crossed your mind: sonna koto zenzen atama ni nakatta.

example.romaji: kare, sakkaa no koto shika atama ni nai n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、サッカーのことしか頭にないんだよ。
example.english: Football's all he ever thinks about.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa sakkaa no koto shika atama ni nai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はサッカーのことしか頭にないんですよ。
examplePolite.english: Football's all he ever thinks about.

entry.notes: Also zenzen atama ni nakatta (it never crossed my mind).

entry.use: Said as X wa ni no tsugi, usually criticising someone's priorities: looks, money, studying or family pushed to second place.

example.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n da yo.
example.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんだよ。
example.english: With him, his family always comes second.

examplePolite.romaji: kare no baai, kazoku wa ni no tsugi na n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼の場合、家族は二の次なんですよ。
examplePolite.english: With him, his family always comes second.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: atomawashi (put off till later).

entry.politeJa: その手には乗りません
entry.use: A playful or wary comeback when someone tries a trick, flattery or bait you've seen before. Te here means a trick or move, as in a game.

example.romaji: mata sore? sono te ni wa noranai yo.
example.ja: またそれ？その手には乗らないよ。
example.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

examplePolite.romaji: mata sore desu ka? sono te ni wa norimasen yo.
examplePolite.ja: またそれですか？その手には乗りませんよ。
examplePolite.english: That again? I'm not falling for it.

entry.notes: Also sono te ga atta! (oh, that's an option!).

entry.use: Said mostly in the past about someone who did something wrong for money or a prize: okane ni me ga kuranda. It also literally means dazzled by light, or dizzy.

example.romaji: kare, okane ni me ga kuranda n da yo.
example.ja: 彼、お金に目がくらんだんだよ。
example.english: He was blinded by the money.

examplePolite.romaji: kare wa okane ni me ga kuranda n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 彼はお金に目がくらんだんですよ。
examplePolite.english: He was blinded by the money.

literal: what kind of turn of the wind

entry.ja: どういう風の吹き回し
entry.kana: どういうかぜのふきまわし
entry.literal: what kind of turn of the wind
entry.use: A teasing question when someone does something nice or out of character, like cooking, paying or cleaning, said with a smile.

example.romaji: ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi?
example.ja: おごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回し？
example.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

examplePolite.romaji: ogotte kureru nante, dou iu kaze no fukimawashi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: おごってくれるなんて、どういう風の吹き回しですか？
examplePolite.english: You're treating me? What's gotten into you?

entry.use: A hunch that turned out right, usually about bad news or someone close, often named afterwards: mushi no shirase ka na. The mushi is the old idea of a bug inside you that senses things. Ki no sei is the opposite: a feeling that turns out to be nothing.

example.romaji: mushi no shirase ka na. kyuu ni denwa shitaku natta n da.
example.ja: 虫の知らせかな。急に電話したくなったんだ。
example.english: Call it a premonition. I suddenly felt like calling.

examplePolite.romaji: mushi no shirase deshou ka. kyuu ni denwa shitaku natta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 虫の知らせでしょうか。急に電話したくなったんです。
examplePolite.english: Call it a premonition. I suddenly felt like calling.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: iya na yokan (a bad feeling).

english: on the tip of my tongue
literal: it's come out as far as the throat

entry.kana: のどまででかかってる
entry.politeJa: 喉まで出かかっています
entry.english: on the tip of my tongue
entry.literal: it's come out as far as the throat
entry.englishIdiom: on the tip of my tongue
entry.use: Said while you're straining to remember a name or word, usually after are, nan datta kke... It's about yourself, in the -teru form.

example.romaji: are, nan datta kke... nodo made dekakatteru n da kedo.
example.ja: あれ、何だったっけ…喉まで出かかってるんだけど。
example.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

examplePolite.romaji: are, nan deshita kke... nodo made dekakatte iru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: あれ、何でしたっけ…喉まで出かかっているんですけど。
examplePolite.english: What was it... it's on the tip of my tongue.

entry.notes: Also koko made dekakatteru (with a hand at the throat).

entry.use: Said while studying, reading or listening when you're tired or distracted and nothing stays, with the material as the subject. Atama ga mawaranai is not being able to think at all; atama ni ireru is the other side, making yourself take it in.

example.romaji: nemukute, zenzen atama ni hairanai.
example.ja: 眠くて、全然頭に入らない。
example.english: I'm so sleepy nothing's going in.

examplePolite.romaji: nemukute, zenzen atama ni hairimasen.
examplePolite.ja: 眠くて、全然頭に入りません。
examplePolite.english: I'm so sleepy nothing's going in.

english: keep in mind, take it in

entry.english: keep in mind, take it in
entry.use: Mostly a request before something important: kore dake wa atama ni irete oite (just keep this in mind). It also means memorising facts or a route: chizu o atama ni ireru.

example.romaji: kore dake wa atama ni iretoite.
example.ja: これだけは頭に入れといて。
example.english: Just keep this one thing in mind.

examplePolite.romaji: kore dake wa atama ni irete oite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: これだけは頭に入れておいてください。
examplePolite.english: Please just keep this one thing in mind.

english: come to your senses, wake up to reality

entry.english: come to your senses, wake up to reality
entry.use: Said to someone fooled by a partner, a scam or their own wishful thinking: ii kagen me o samashite! About yourself it's me ga sameta (I've come to my senses). The same words literally mean wake up from sleep, which the collocation list covers as me ga sameru.

example.romaji: ii kagen me o samashite! damasareteru yo.
example.ja: いい加減目を覚まして！騙されてるよ。
example.english: Wake up! You're being played.

examplePolite.romaji: ii kagen me o samashite kudasai. damasarete imasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: いい加減目を覚ましてください。騙されていますよ。
examplePolite.english: Please wake up. You're being played.

entry.notes: Rough command: me o samase!

entry.use: Two senses: something too gripping to stop watching (a close match, a drama's final episode), or someone who needs constant watching (a toddler, a reckless friend). Me o hanasu na is the warning not to look away.

example.romaji: kono shiai, saigo made me ga hanasenai ne.
example.ja: この試合、最後まで目が離せないね。
example.english: You can't take your eyes off this match.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shiai wa saigo made me ga hanasemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: この試合は最後まで目が離せませんね。
examplePolite.english: You can't take your eyes off this match.

entry.use: Said of someone watching for trouble or rule-breaking: parents, teachers, a strict boss, the police. You'll hear it in the -teru form. Me ga hanasenai is needing to watch; me o hikaraseru is standing guard.

example.romaji: buchou ga me o hikaraseteru kara, sumaho tsukaenai.
example.ja: 部長が目を光らせてるから、スマホ使えない。
example.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

examplePolite.romaji: buchou ga me o hikarasete iru node, sumaho wa tsukaemasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: 部長が目を光らせているので、スマホは使えませんね。
examplePolite.english: The boss is watching like a hawk, so no phones.

entry.use: The thing is the subject and it draws attention by standing out: a sign, an outfit, a bright colour. Hitome o hiku is drawing other people's looks. Me ni tsuku is just noticing, often something you'd rather not.

example.romaji: ano kanban, sugoku me o hiku ne.
example.ja: あの看板、すごく目を引くね。
example.english: That sign really grabs your attention.

examplePolite.romaji: ano kanban wa sugoku me o hikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: あの看板はすごく目を引きますね。
examplePolite.english: That sign really grabs your attention.

entry.use: Said when your eyes keep drifting to something, often with tsui and -chau: tsui X ni me ga itchau. The negative me ga ikanakatta means you didn't notice it at all.

example.romaji: tsui hito no kutsu ni me ga itchau.
example.ja: つい人の靴に目が行っちゃう。
example.english: I always end up looking at people's shoes.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui hito no kutsu ni me ga itte shimaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: つい人の靴に目が行ってしまいます。
examplePolite.english: I always end up looking at people's shoes.

english: look away from, refuse to face

entry.english: look away from, refuse to face
entry.use: Said about avoiding an unpleasant truth: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide. It's also literal, turning your eyes from something painful to see. Mite minu furi is ignoring someone else's trouble; me o somukeru is avoiding facing it yourself.

example.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide.
example.ja: 現実から目を背けないで。
example.english: Stop running away from reality.

examplePolite.romaji: genjitsu kara me o somukenaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 現実から目を背けないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't run away from reality.

romaji: mune ni te o atete kangaeru

literal: think with a hand on your chest

entry.polite: mune ni te o atete kangaemasu

entry.politeJa: 胸に手を当てて考えます
entry.english: think honestly about what you did
entry.literal: think with a hand on your chest
entry.use: A scolding line to someone who claims not to know why you're upset. It's almost always a request in the -te mite form: jibun no mune ni te o atete kangaete mite.

examplePolite.romaji: jibun no mune ni te o atete kangaete mite kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: 自分の胸に手を当てて考えてみてください。
examplePolite.english: Put your hand on your heart and think about it.

entry.use: Said when a comparison, a chart or a before-and-after makes the answer instantly clear, often after mireba (if you look). It's used with da or desu.

example.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen da yo.
example.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然だよ。
example.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

examplePolite.romaji: narabete mireba ichimoku ryouzen desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 並べてみれば一目瞭然ですよ。
examplePolite.english: Put them side by side and it's obvious.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: mireba wakaru (you'll see if you look).

english: a temptation you'd better not see

entry.english: a temptation you'd better not see
entry.use: A joking line about something tempting you can't or shouldn't have: cake while dieting, a gadget you can't afford. It's said with da: kore wa me no doku da.

example.romaji: daietto chuu ni kore wa me no doku da yo.

example.english: That's torture to look at when I'm on a diet.

examplePolite.romaji: daietto chuu ni kore wa me no doku desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ダイエット中にこれは目の毒ですよ。
examplePolite.english: That's torture to look at when I'm on a diet.

entry.englishIdiom: in one ear and out the other
entry.use: Said about words that go straight through someone: a lecture, advice, a long speech. It's also said of money that comes in and goes straight out (kyuuryou ga migi kara hidari).

example.romaji: kouchou no hanashi, zenbu migi kara hidari datta.

example.english: The principal's speech went in one ear and out the other.

examplePolite.english: The principal's speech went in one ear and out the other.

entry.use: Said with disapproval about someone whose choices baffle you: X suru hito no ki ga shirenai (I don't get people who X). It's about a person or a type of person; dou ka shiteru says they've lost it.

example.romaji: konna samui no ni oyogu hito no ki ga shirenai.
example.ja: こんな寒いのに泳ぐ人の気が知れない。
example.english: I don't get people who swim when it's this cold.

examplePolite.romaji: konna ni samui no ni oyogu hito no ki ga shiremasen ne.
examplePolite.ja: こんなに寒いのに泳ぐ人の気が知れませんね。
examplePolite.english: I don't get people who swim when it's this cold.

english: think ahead too much, read into things

entry.english: think ahead too much, read into things
entry.use: Said when someone anticipates needs or reads too much into things, kindly or needlessly: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii yo. Ki o kubaru is plain attentiveness, always a compliment.

example.romaji: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii yo.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna ni ki o mawasanakute ii desu yo.

examplePolite.romaji: konna koto ni naru to wa, omoi mo yorimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: こんなことになるとは、思いもよりませんでした。
examplePolite.english: I never imagined it would come to this.

entry.notes: Casual: omoi mo shinakatta (never even thought of it).

english: weigh on your mind, nag at you

entry.english: weigh on your mind, nag at you
entry.use: For a worry or a small detail that keeps nagging: chotto ki ni kakaru koto ga aru (something's bothering me). It's heavier and lasts longer than ki ni naru.

examplePolite.romaji: kanojo no sakki no kotoba ga ki ni kakaru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 彼女のさっきの言葉が気にかかるんです。
examplePolite.english: What she said earlier is weighing on my mind.

entry.notes: Close: ki ni naru (be curious about, bother you).

english: be naive, not think it through

entry.english: be naive, not think it through
entry.use: A blunt judgement on a plan that ignores how hard things are, usually from someone more experienced: sonna no kangae ga amai yo. Amaku miru is underestimating one task or opponent.

examplePolite.english: Done in a day? That's naive.

english: it depends how you look at it
literal: things are as you think them

entry.english: it depends how you look at it
entry.literal: things are as you think them
entry.use: Said to cheer someone up by finding a better angle on a setback, then giving that angle. It's a stock phrase, always with da or desu.

example.romaji: mono wa kangaeyou da yo. ii keiken ni natta jan.
example.ja: ものは考えようだよ。いい経験になったじゃん。
example.english: It's how you look at it. It was good experience.

examplePolite.romaji: mono wa kangaeyou desu yo. ii keiken ni natta ja nai desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: ものは考えようですよ。いい経験になったじゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: It's how you look at it. It was good experience.

romaji: nen ni wa nen o ireru
literal: put care on top of care

entry.romaji: nen ni wa nen o ireru
entry.polite: nen ni wa nen o iremasu
entry.kana: ねんにはねんをいれる
entry.literal: put care on top of care
entry.use: Said when you check again or take an extra precaution though it's probably fine. You'll mostly hear the -te form, nen ni wa nen o irete, or just nen ni wa nen o.

example.romaji: nen ni wa nen o irete, mou ikkai kakunin shiyou.
example.ja: 念には念を入れて、もう一回確認しよう。
example.english: Just to be extra safe, let's check once more.

examplePolite.romaji: nen ni wa nen o irete, mou ichido kakunin shimashou.
examplePolite.ja: 念には念を入れて、もう一度確認しましょう。
examplePolite.english: Just to be extra safe, let's check once more.

entry.notes: Short version: nen no tame (just in case).

romaji: nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii
literal: want it so much a hand comes out of the throat

entry.romaji: nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii
entry.polite: nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii desu
entry.ja: 喉から手が出るほど欲しい
entry.kana: のどからてがでるほどほしい
entry.politeJa: 喉から手が出るほど欲しいです
entry.literal: want it so much a hand comes out of the throat
entry.use: Said about something you want badly but can't easily get: a rare item, a ticket, a job, a player a team needs. It's always with hodo hoshii, and people often stop at nodo kara te ga deru hodo.

example.romaji: ano chiketto, nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii.
example.ja: あのチケット、喉から手が出るほど欲しい。
example.english: I'd give anything for that ticket.

examplePolite.romaji: ano chiketto, nodo kara te ga deru hodo hoshii desu.
examplePolite.ja: あのチケット、喉から手が出るほど欲しいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd give anything for that ticket.

entry.use: Said right after a near miss, from a car that nearly hit you to a scolding you just avoided: inochibiroi shita. Almost always past, and used half-jokingly for small escapes too.

example.romaji: abunakatta, inochibiroi shita yo
example.ja: 危なかった、命拾いしたよ
example.english: That was close. I got lucky there.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni inochibiroi shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 本当に命拾いしました
examplePolite.english: I really had a lucky escape.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: tasukatta (that saved me).

entry.use: The groan when someone else gets there first: the last item, a seat, a confession, a promotion, a rival company's launch. Mostly past and often without o: saki kosareta! For getting in first on purpose, say sente o utsu.

example.romaji: aa, saki kosareta!
example.ja: あー、先越された！
example.english: Argh, someone beat me to it!

examplePolite.romaji: tasha ni saki o kosarete shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 他社に先を越されてしまいました
examplePolite.english: Another company beat us to it.

entry.notes: Rarer active form: saki o kosu (get there ahead of someone).

english: act first, get in before the other side
literal: play the first move (in shogi or go)

entry.english: act first, get in before the other side
entry.literal: play the first move (in shogi or go)
entry.use: Said about heading off a problem or a rival before they move, like complaints, a competitor or a parent's objection. Mostly advice (sente o utte okou) or past (sente o utareta, they got in first). It shares te (a move) with te o utsu.

example.romaji: monku iwareru mae ni sente utte okou
example.ja: 文句言われる前に先手打っておこう
example.english: Let's get in first, before they complain.

examplePolite.romaji: kujou ga kuru mae ni, sente o utte okimashou
examplePolite.ja: 苦情が来る前に、先手を打っておきましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's act before any complaints come in.

entry.notes: Opposite feeling: saki o kosareru (someone beat you to it).

english: throw away (a chance, a career, years)

entry.english: throw away (a chance, a career, years)
entry.use: Said about wasting something big through one bad choice: jinsei o bou ni furu (throw your life away), chansu o bou ni furu. Often a warning: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo. For effort that simply comes to nothing, say mizu no awa.

example.romaji: sonna koto de jinsei bou ni furu na yo
example.ja: そんなことで人生棒に振るなよ
example.english: Don't throw your life away over that.

examplePolite.romaji: sekkaku no chansu o bou ni futte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: せっかくのチャンスを棒に振ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I threw away a golden chance.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: muda ni suru (waste).

literal: the second dance (a clown copying the first dancer)

entry.literal: the second dance (a clown copying the first dancer)
entry.use: Almost always X no ni no mai ni naru, usually as a warning: senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni (so you don't end up like your senpai). X is the person or event whose mistake you'd repeat. Don't confuse it with ni no ashi o fumu (hesitate).

example.romaji: senpai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni ne
example.ja: 先輩の二の舞にならないようにね
example.english: Don't end up like your senpai, OK?

examplePolite.romaji: zenkai no ni no mai ni naranai you ni shimashou
examplePolite.ja: 前回の二の舞にならないようにしましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's not repeat what happened last time.

entry.notes: Formal: ni no mai o enjiru (repeat the same mistake).

english: get on track, start running smoothly

entry.english: get on track, start running smoothly
entry.use: Said about a business, a project or a new life once it starts running smoothly, usually as yatto kidou ni notte kita (it's finally on track). Unlike choushi ni noru, there's nothing cocky about it.

example.romaji: mise mo yatto kidou ni notte kita yo
example.ja: 店もやっと軌道に乗ってきたよ
example.english: The shop's finally getting on its feet.

examplePolite.romaji: mise mo yatto kidou ni notte kimashita
examplePolite.ja: 店もやっと軌道に乗ってきました
examplePolite.english: The shop is finally on track.

entry.notes: Literal twin: going into orbit.

literal: go back to the starting square (of a board game)

entry.literal: go back to the starting square (of a board game)
entry.use: Said when a setback wipes out all progress on a plan, a search or a negotiation, mostly in the past: mata furidashi ni modotta. furidashi ni modoru is what happens to you; ichi kara yarinaosu is what you then choose to do.

example.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modotchatta
example.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻っちゃった
example.english: Now we're back to square one.

examplePolite.romaji: kore de mata furidashi ni modorimashita ne
examplePolite.ja: これでまた振り出しに戻りましたね
examplePolite.english: So we're back to square one again.

entry.notes: Scrapping a plan on purpose is hakushi ni modosu.

entry.use: Said after lost work or a failed plan, and about making a fresh start in life. The noun form is just as common: ichi kara yarinaoshi da (back to the beginning).

example.romaji: zenbu kiechatta, ichi kara yarinaoshi da yo
example.ja: 全部消えちゃった、一からやり直しだよ
example.english: It all got deleted. I have to start from scratch.

examplePolite.romaji: zenbu kiete shimatte, ichi kara yarinaoshi desu
examplePolite.ja: 全部消えてしまって、一からやり直しです
examplePolite.english: Everything got deleted, so I have to start from scratch.

entry.notes: Variant: ichi kara denaosu (make a fresh start, of a person).

entry.kana: あぶないはしをわたる
entry.use: Mostly said when refusing a risky or shady plan: sonna abunai hashi wa wataranai (I won't take that kind of risk). It's usually about money or bending rules, not physical danger.

example.romaji: sonna abunai hashi, wataritakunai yo
example.ja: そんな危ない橋、渡りたくないよ
example.english: I don't want to take a risk like that.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna abunai hashi wa wataritakunai desu
examplePolite.ja: そんな危ない橋は渡りたくないです
examplePolite.english: I'd rather not take that kind of risk.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: risuku ga takai (it's too risky).

english: dig your own grave, give yourself away

entry.english: dig your own grave, give yourself away
entry.use: Said when someone makes things worse for themselves, most often by talking too much and giving themselves away: jibun de boketsu hotta. Common as a self-mocking groan.

example.romaji: yokei na koto itte boketsu hotta
example.ja: 余計なこと言って墓穴掘った
example.english: I said too much and dug my own grave.

examplePolite.romaji: yokei na koto o itte, boketsu o hotte shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: 余計なことを言って、墓穴を掘ってしまいました
examplePolite.english: I said too much and dug myself a hole.

entry.notes: Same idea: jibun no kubi o shimeru (tighten the noose on yourself).

entry.use: Said when two things are separated by almost nothing: a win and a loss, a near miss (kami hitoe de tasukatta), or the set line tensai to baka wa kami hitoe (genius and idiot are a hair apart).

example.romaji: tensai to baka wa kami hitoe tte iu yo ne
example.ja: 天才とバカは紙一重って言うよね
example.english: They say there's a fine line between genius and idiot.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou ni kami hitoe deshita ne
examplePolite.ja: 本当に紙一重でしたね
examplePolite.english: That really came down to a hair.

entry.notes: Near-twin: kan ippatsu (by a hair).

entry.englishIdiom: get too big for one's boots
entry.use: The standard rebuke for someone smug after a little success or praise: ii ki ni naru na yo. It sounds sharper than choushi ni noru, which can be playful. Don't confuse it with ki ni naru (be on one's mind).

example.romaji: chotto homerareta kurai de ii ki ni naru na yo
example.ja: ちょっと褒められたくらいでいい気になるなよ
example.english: Don't get full of yourself over a little praise.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ii ki ni natte imashita
examplePolite.ja: ちょっといい気になっていました
examplePolite.english: I was getting a bit full of myself.

entry.notes: Sarcastic cousin: ii ki na mon da (must be nice).

entry.use: A warning about a mistake or scandal serious enough to cost someone their job: baretara kubi ga tobu yo. Mostly future or conditional; for someone already fired, say kubi ni natta.

example.romaji: konna misu baretara kubi ga tobu yo
example.ja: こんなミスバレたらクビが飛ぶよ
example.english: If this mistake gets out, heads will roll.

examplePolite.romaji: kore ga baretara kubi ga tobimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: これがバレたらクビが飛びますよ
examplePolite.english: If this gets out, someone's losing their job.

entry.notes: Literal twin: a real beheading in period dramas.

entry.use: Said about not forcing a plan, a relationship or a career and seeing where it goes: ato wa nagare ni makaseyou. It sounds relaxed, not lazy.

example.romaji: maa, ato wa nagare ni makaseyou
example.ja: まあ、あとは流れに任せよう
example.english: Well, let's just see where it goes from here.

examplePolite.romaji: ato wa nagare ni makasemashou
examplePolite.ja: あとは流れに任せましょう
examplePolite.english: Let's let things take their course from here.

entry.notes: Same meaning: nariyuki makase.

literal: the back face (of the die) comes up

entry.literal: the back face (of the die) comes up
entry.use: Said when a plan or a kind gesture produces the opposite of what you wanted, almost always in the past: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni deta (I meant well, but it backfired).

example.romaji: yokare to omotte yatta noni, urame ni deta
example.ja: 良かれと思ってやったのに、裏目に出た
example.english: I meant well, but it backfired.

examplePolite.romaji: yokare to omotte shita koto ga urame ni demashita
examplePolite.ja: 良かれと思ってしたことが裏目に出ました
examplePolite.english: What I did with good intentions backfired.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: gyaku kouka (counterproductive).

english: get stuck with the worst job or role

entry.english: get stuck with the worst job or role
entry.use: The grumble when you end up with the job, role or seat nobody wanted, through bad luck or being too nice: mata binbou kuji hiichatta. hame ni naru is about the chore itself; binbou kuji is about being the unlucky one.

example.romaji: mata binbou kuji hiichatta yo
example.ja: また貧乏くじ引いちゃったよ
example.english: I got stuck with the short straw again.

examplePolite.romaji: mata binbou kuji o hiite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: また貧乏くじを引いてしまいました
examplePolite.english: I drew the short straw again.

english: something came over me (a sudden lapse)

entry.english: something came over me (a sudden lapse)
entry.use: The set excuse for an out-of-character lapse, like cheating, pocketing something or a cruel remark, almost always as tsui ma ga sashita (something just came over me). Said about yourself, or to excuse someone else.

example.romaji: gomen, tsui ma ga sashita n da
example.ja: ごめん、つい魔が差したんだ
example.english: Sorry, something just came over me.

examplePolite.romaji: tsui ma ga sashite shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: つい魔が差してしまいました
examplePolite.english: I gave in to temptation for a moment.

entry.notes: Unrelated to ma ga warui (bad timing) despite the shared sound ma.

english: it worked out in the end, so fine

entry.english: it worked out in the end, so fine
entry.use: Said when luck covered a mistake or a messy process: maa, kekka oorai jan. Casual and a bit cheeky, often used to brush off criticism of how you got there.

example.romaji: maa, kekka oorai jan
example.ja: まあ、結果オーライじゃん
example.english: Well, it worked out in the end.

examplePolite.romaji: kekka oorai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 結果オーライですね
examplePolite.english: Well, it all worked out.

entry.notes: oorai is 'all right', the fielder's call in baseball.

entry.politeJa: 踏んだり蹴ったりです
entry.use: The casual bad-day summary when several bad things pile up: kyou wa fundari kettari da. Said mostly about yourself, usually after listing the mishaps.

example.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari da yo
example.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりだよ
example.english: Today's been one thing after another.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hontou ni fundari kettari deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に踏んだり蹴ったりでした
examplePolite.english: Today was one thing after another.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: tsuitenai (I'm out of luck).

english: the third try will be the one
literal: the third time is the honest one

entry.kana: さんどめのしょうじき
entry.english: the third try will be the one
entry.literal: the third time is the honest one
entry.use: Said before a third attempt at an exam, a confession or a game, or after it finally works: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da. It is the hopeful answer to nido aru koto wa sando aru.

example.romaji: kondo koso sandome no shoujiki da!
example.ja: 今度こそ三度目の正直だ！
example.english: Third time's the charm!

examplePolite.romaji: sandome no shoujiki de, yatto goukaku shimashita
examplePolite.ja: 三度目の正直で、やっと合格しました
examplePolite.english: Third time lucky, I finally passed.

entry.use: The stock complaint about pay, bonuses, pensions or interest: boonasu wa suzume no namida hodo. Said about money, not other small amounts.

example.romaji: boonasu, suzume no namida datta yo
example.ja: ボーナス、雀の涙だったよ
example.english: My bonus was a pittance.

examplePolite.romaji: boonasu wa suzume no namida deshita
examplePolite.ja: ボーナスは雀の涙でした
examplePolite.english: The bonus was next to nothing.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: hon no sukoshi (just a tiny bit).

entry.use: Almost always hotobori ga sameru made (until it blows over), about lying low after a scandal, a fight or a gaffe.

example.romaji: hotobori ga sameru made, shibaraku otonashiku shitoko
example.ja: ほとぼりが冷めるまで、しばらくおとなしくしとこ
example.english: Let's keep a low profile till it blows over.

examplePolite.romaji: hotobori ga sameru made matta hou ga ii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: ほとぼりが冷めるまで待った方がいいですよ
examplePolite.english: Better wait until it blows over.

english: your own fault, you brought it on yourself
literal: rust that came out of the blade itself

entry.english: your own fault, you brought it on yourself
entry.literal: rust that came out of the blade itself
entry.use: A saying for trouble someone caused themselves, often said about yourself with a rueful laugh: mi kara deta sabi da ne. Softer and more self-aware than jigou jitoku.

example.romaji: maa, mi kara deta sabi da ne
example.ja: まあ、身から出た錆だね
example.english: Well, it's my own fault.

examplePolite.romaji: mi kara deta sabi desu kara, shikata arimasen
examplePolite.ja: 身から出た錆ですから、仕方ありません
examplePolite.english: It's my own fault, so there's nothing to be done.

entry.notes: Four-character twin: jigou jitoku.

entry.use: Said about a clumsy mistake that spoils something, mostly in the past and often about yourself: doji funda. In polite talk it's a self-deprecating admission: tonda doji o funde shimaimashita.

example.romaji: yabai, doji funda
example.ja: やばい、ドジ踏んだ
example.english: Ugh, I blew it.

examplePolite.romaji: tonda doji o funde shimaimashita
examplePolite.ja: とんだドジを踏んでしまいました
examplePolite.english: I made a silly blunder.

entry.notes: Casual verb: dojiru (dojitta); a clumsy person is a doji.

english: a godsend, just what you'd hoped for
literal: not even (something) you'd dare wish for

entry.english: a godsend, just what you'd hoped for
entry.literal: not even (something) you'd dare wish for
entry.use: Almost always before a noun: negatte mo nai chansu / hanashi (a chance you couldn't have hoped for). Said when an offer or a bit of luck is better than you'd dared to hope.

example.romaji: sore, negatte mo nai chansu jan
example.ja: それ、願ってもないチャンスじゃん
example.english: That's the chance of a lifetime!

examplePolite.romaji: negatte mo nai ohanashi desu
examplePolite.ja: 願ってもないお話です
examplePolite.english: That's a wonderful offer.

english: can't afford it, out of reach

entry.english: can't afford it, out of reach
entry.use: Said mostly while shopping or window-shopping: takakute te ga denai. It can also mean a task is beyond you (muzukashikute te ga denai). The positive te ga deru usually means 'lash out, start hitting'.

example.romaji: ii kedo, takakute te ga denai yo
example.ja: いいけど、高くて手が出ないよ
example.english: It's nice, but way out of my price range.

examplePolite.romaji: ii n desu kedo, takakute te ga demasen
examplePolite.ja: いいんですけど、高くて手が出ません
examplePolite.english: It's nice, but it's too expensive for me.

entry.notes: Plain alternative: takakute kaenai (too expensive to buy).

english: take proper responsibility; draw a clear line

entry.english: take proper responsibility; draw a clear line
entry.use: Two everyday uses: owning up to a mess properly, often by apologising or resigning (kejime o tsukenai to), and keeping things clearly apart, like work and private life (kouji no kejime). keri o tsukeru ends a matter; kejime is about doing it properly.

example.romaji: kono ken wa chanto kejime tsukenai to
example.ja: この件はちゃんとけじめつけないと
example.english: I need to take proper responsibility for this.

examplePolite.romaji: kono ken wa kichinto kejime o tsukemasu
examplePolite.ja: この件はきちんとけじめをつけます
examplePolite.english: I'll take proper responsibility for this matter.

entry.notes: kouji no kejime: keeping work and private life apart.

english: an offer too good to be true

entry.english: an offer too good to be true
entry.use: Said about deals, jobs and investments that sound suspicious, nearly always with doubt: sonna umai hanashi aru wake nai (there's no way that's real), or umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (every sweet deal has a catch).

example.romaji: sonna umai hanashi, aru wake nai jan
example.ja: そんなうまい話、あるわけないじゃん
example.english: There's no way a deal that good is real.

examplePolite.romaji: sonna umai hanashi wa nai to omoimasu yo
examplePolite.ja: そんなうまい話はないと思いますよ
examplePolite.english: I doubt a deal that good really exists.

entry.notes: Saying: umai hanashi ni wa ura ga aru (a sweet deal always has a catch).

english: end up the loser, get nothing for your trouble

entry.english: end up the loser, get nothing for your trouble
entry.use: Said when doing the right or trusting thing leaves you worse off: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru (those who play it straight lose out). Don't confuse it with baka ni suru (make fun of) or baka ni naranai (costs add up).

example.romaji: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru n da yo ne
example.ja: 真面目にやった方がバカを見るんだよね
example.english: The ones who play it straight always lose out.

examplePolite.romaji: majime ni yatta hou ga baka o miru n desu yo ne
examplePolite.ja: 真面目にやった方がバカを見るんですよね
examplePolite.english: Those who do things properly end up losing out.

entry.notes: Saying: shoujikimono ga baka o miru (honesty doesn't pay).

english: be on a roll; ride a trend

entry.english: be on a roll; ride a trend
entry.use: Said of a team, a business or a person on a good run, usually nami ni notteru, or of catching a trend: jidai no nami ni noru. Unlike choushi ni noru, it's praise.

example.romaji: ano chiimu, ima nami ni notteru ne
example.ja: あのチーム、今波に乗ってるね
example.english: That team's on a roll right now.

examplePolite.romaji: ano chiimu wa ima nami ni notte imasu ne
examplePolite.ja: あのチームは今波に乗っていますね
examplePolite.english: That team is really on a roll at the moment.

entry.notes: Literal twin: riding an actual wave.
